screens.title: Environmental Sensors: Temperature, Humidity, Light, and Gas
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on the everyday sensors you’ll use to sense temperature, humidity, light, and common gases. You will learn what each sensor measures, how it represents that measurement as a voltage or a digital message, and why reading the right signal matters when you convert a number into degrees, percent, or a safety alert. We’ll use analog examples like the TMP36 and LM35 that give a voltage proportional to temperature, and digital examples like the DHT11 and DHT22 that send humidity and temperature as a timed data packet. You’ll also see how an LDR works inside a voltage divider to report light, and how an MQ-2 reports gas concentration on an analog output after a warm-up period. I’ll explain where a datasheet gives you the conversion formulas, and how a library safely hides timing details for digital sensors. By the end of this chapter you’ll be able to wire a sensor, choose analog versus digital reading, install a library, and convert raw readings into a human-friendly value. Think about a simple weather logger or a safety alarm — these are direct applications of what you’ll build here.

Environmental Sensors

Understand how TMP36, LM35, DHT11/DHT22, LDRs, and MQ-2 produce signals and how to convert those signals into meaningful readings.

Analog sensors give a voltage; digital sensors send timed data. Choose the correct read method.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives give you practical, testable skills. First, you will interface with analog temperature sensors like the TMP36 and LM35 so you can convert a measured voltage into degrees Celsius. This matters because raw voltages are not intuitive until you apply the sensor's scale and offset from the datasheet. Second, you will use digital sensors such as the DHT11 and DHT22 to read temperature and humidity using a library. The library handles precise timing and produces reliable values; you will learn how to install and call the functions in your sketch. Third, you will read light levels using a light-dependent resistor inside a voltage divider. That teaches you how resistance maps to voltage and how simple calibration produces percentages or thresholds for real projects. Fourth, you will learn to use sensor datasheets and libraries: how to find conversion formulas, warm-up requirements, and wiring notes so your measurements are accurate and repeatable. Each objective includes a practical milestone so you can verify competency and build a simple monitoring circuit confidently.

screens.title: Analog vs. Digital Sensors
screens.narratorSegment: Sensors present the physical world as electrical values in two common forms: analog voltages or digital data. An analog sensor changes its output voltage continuously as the measured quantity changes. For example, the TMP36 outputs a voltage that rises linearly with temperature. The Arduino’s analog-to-digital converter samples that voltage and turns it into an integer between zero and 1023 on a five-volt board. Digital sensors, like the DHT11 and DHT22, transmit encoded data over a single wire in timed pulses rather than presenting a continuous voltage. The microcontroller needs to follow that protocol or use a library that does. The practical difference matters when you wire and read the part: analog sensors typically need a stable reference, and digital sensors need correct timing or a library. A common misconception is that all sensors can be read with analogRead; digital sensors require protocol handling. A quick example: the TMP36’s analog voltage can be converted directly into degrees using the datasheet formula, while a DHT11 requires a library call that returns humidity and temperature. Takeaway: choose the read method that matches the sensor’s signal type so your code and wiring produce meaningful numbers.

keyIdea.title: Signal types matter
keyIdea.text: Analog outputs become voltages the ADC converts to integers; digital sensors send structured data that usually needs a library.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Analog vs Digital
Definition

Analog outputs

A sensor that varies its voltage with the measured condition. The Arduino reads the voltage with analogRead and converts the ADC value to a voltage using the board reference.

Key formula
Voltage = (reading / 1023.0) × Vref
Concrete example
TMP36 gives 750 mV at 25°C; scale is 10 mV per °C with a 500 mV offset.
Common mistake
Reading a digital sensor with analogRead will return meaningless voltages or floating values; use the correct protocol.
Definition

Digital outputs

A sensor that communicates using a defined protocol over one or more wires. DHT sensors send timed pulses representing humidity and temperature values; you normally use a library to parse them.

Why libraries help
Libraries implement precise timing and parsing, avoiding fragile manual implementations that often fail under load.
Takeaway
Match your read method to the sensor type: analogRead for voltages, library calls for timed digital protocols.

screens.title: Reading TMP36: Formula and Example
screens.narratorSegment: The TMP36 is an analog temperature sensor whose output is a voltage that changes linearly with temperature. The datasheet gives two important facts: at 25 degrees Celsius the output is 750 millivolts, and the sensor scales approximately 10 millivolts per degree. Practically, on a standard five-volt Arduino, you read an ADC value, convert it to a voltage by dividing by 1023 and multiplying by five, then apply the TMP36 formula. For example, subtract the 500 millivolt offset and multiply by 100 to get degrees Celsius. A common misunderstanding is to forget the offset; using the wrong formula will shift every reading by several degrees. The example code shown produces an integer reading, computes voltage, then temperature in Celsius. Try the short mental test: given 0.73 volts from a TMP36, the formula leads to 23 degrees C when you subtract 0.5 and multiply by 100. This screen shows the code and explains each step so you can confidently translate ADC numbers into human-friendly temperatures. Reading TMP36: Formula and Example means convert adc to voltage, apply the tmp36 offset and scale from the datasheet to get temperature in celsius.. In practical terms, convert adc reading to celsius with the tmp36 scale. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: TMP36 conversion
keyIdea.text: Convert ADC to voltage, apply the TMP36 offset and scale from the datasheet to get temperature in Celsius.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › TMP36
Code Example
int reading = analogRead(A0);
float voltage = (reading / 1023.0) * 5.0;
float temperatureC = (voltage - 0.5) * 100.0;
Step 1 — ADC to voltage
Divide the ADC reading by 1023 and scale by Vref (5.0 V) to get voltage in volts.
Step 2 — Apply TMP36 formula
Subtract 0.5 V offset, then multiply by 100 to convert volts to degrees Celsius.
Explanation & Example
Given a measured voltage of 0.73 volts from the TMP36, subtract the 0.5 volt offset to get 0.23, then multiply by 100 to get 23°C. Forgetting the 0.5 offset creates a consistent error in the entire reading range.
Takeaway
Use the datasheet’s scale and offset. Check your math with a known temperature point to validate wiring and reference voltage.

screens.title: TMP36 vs LM35
screens.narratorSegment: TMP36 and LM35 are both analog temperature sensors commonly used with Arduino, and both scale at about 10 millivolts per degree Celsius. The crucial practical difference is the presence of an offset with the TMP36 and none with the LM35. The TMP36 specifies an offset so its output is roughly 0.5 volts at zero degrees, which simplifies single-supply designs but requires you to subtract that offset when converting voltage to temperature. The LM35, on the other hand, has no offset: its output is near 0 volts at zero degrees, so you multiply the measured voltage by the scale directly. When choosing between them, consult the datasheet for accuracy, operating voltage, and wiring notes — which tells you the correct formula to use. A common error is applying the TMP36 formula to LM35 data or vice versa, producing a systematic temperature error equal to the offset. Use a quick bench check at room temperature to confirm your conversion and avoid that mistake. In practical terms, two similar analog temperature sensors with different offsets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › TMP36 vs LM35
TMP36
Scale: 10 mV per °C with a 500 mV offset. Datasheet examples show 750 mV at 25°C.
Conversion
temperatureC = (voltage - 0.5) × 100
When to use
Good for single-supply designs; remember to apply the offset in software.
LM35
Scale: 10 mV per °C with no offset. Output near 0 V at 0°C according to its datasheet.
Conversion
temperatureC = voltage × 100
Common mistake
Applying TMP36 offset to LM35 gives readings that are too low by about 0.5 V equivalent in degrees.

screens.title: DHT11 and DHT22: Digital Humidity and Temperature
screens.narratorSegment: DHT11 and DHT22 are digital humidity and temperature sensors that communicate over a single data wire using timed pulses. They are not analog voltage outputs, so you cannot use analogRead. Instead, you either implement the precise timing protocol yourself or — more commonly — use a library that handles the timing and parsing for you. The typical flow is: install the DHT library through the Arduino Library Manager, include the library at the top of your sketch, create a sensor object with its pin and type, initialize it in setup, and then call readHumidity and readTemperature in loop. Libraries often provide example sketches you can run to verify wiring. A frequent misconception is that digital sensors are always more accurate; accuracy depends on the sensor model and its specs. DHT22 typically offers higher accuracy and range than DHT11. For learning, rely on example sketches and the library’s functions for consistent readings and error handling. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › DHT11 / DHT22
Protocol Flow
  1. Install the DHT library via the Arduino Library Manager.
  2. Include the library and create a sensor object with the pin and type.
  3. Call the library’s begin method in setup to initialize timing.
  4. In loop, call readHumidity and readTemperature and check for valid values.
Model note
DHT22 generally offers better accuracy and range than DHT11; consult the datasheet before choosing.
Example Wiring & Check
Power the sensor, connect data to a digital pin with a pull-up when required, and run the library example. If the Serial Monitor shows sensible humidity and temperature every two seconds, wiring and code are likely correct.
Common mistake
Skipping the library leads to fragile timing code and unreliable readings under different CPU loads.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › DHT Example
Sketch (visual excerpt)
#include "DHT.h"
#define DHTPIN 2
#define DHTTYPE DHT11
DHT dht(DHTPIN, DHTTYPE);

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  dht.begin();
}

void loop() {
  float h = dht.readHumidity();
  float t = dht.readTemperature();
  Serial.print("Humidity: ");
  Serial.print(h);
  Serial.print("%  Temperature: ");
  Serial.print(t);
  Serial.println("C");
  delay(2000);
}
Guide & Troubleshooting
  • Install the DHT library via Library Manager then open the example sketch to test.
  • Ensure the correct sensor type constant matches your sensor (DHT11 or DHT22).
  • If you see NaN or invalid readings, check wiring, power, and pin assignments before debugging code timing.
Practical tip
Run the example to verify the library and Serial Monitor output, then integrate the calls into your main loop and add error checks.

screens.title: Light-Dependent Resistor (LDR) and Voltage Divider
screens.narratorSegment: An LDR changes its resistance depending on the light level: more light usually reduces resistance, while darkness increases it. Because Arduino’s ADC measures voltage, not resistance, we place the LDR in a voltage divider with a fixed resistor to convert resistance changes into a measurable voltage. The divider produces a voltage between ground and Vcc that varies predictably with the LDR’s resistance. Depending on whether the LDR is tied to the top or bottom of the divider, a brighter environment can produce either a higher or lower voltage. Calibration is essential: map ADC values to percentages or choose a threshold that separates light and dark for your application. A common mistake is to treat raw ADC values as absolute light levels without calibrating for ambient conditions and the chosen fixed resistor. A practical exercise is to read the ADC value in different lighting, record numbers, and pick a threshold that reliably triggers an action like turning an LED on when it’s dark. Light-Dependent Resistor (LDR) and Voltage Divider means use a fixed resistor with the ldr to produce a voltage the adc can read; then calibrate adc values to usable thresholds or percentages.. In practical terms, turning changing resistance into a readable voltage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use a fixed resistor with the LDR to produce a voltage the ADC can read; then calibrate ADC values to usable thresholds or percentages.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › LDR & Divider
How it works
Place the LDR and a resistor in series between Vcc and ground. Read the mid-point voltage with analogRead. The midpoint voltage varies with light because the LDR’s resistance changes.
Calibration steps
Record ADC values in bright and dark conditions, then map range to 0–100% or choose a working threshold for your project.
Concrete example
If your ADC reads 900 in bright light and 120 in darkness, you can compute a percentage using linear mapping or set a threshold, for example below 300 as 'dark'.
Common mistake
Using the wrong fixed resistor can make the voltage range too small. Choose the resistor to produce a useful voltage span across expected lighting conditions.

screens.title: MQ-2 Gas Sensor
screens.narratorSegment: MQ-2 is a family of gas sensors that detect combustible gases such as propane, methane, and smoke by producing an analog voltage proportional to gas concentration. These sensors are often easy to wire: power, ground, and an analog output to an ADC pin. However, they require a warm-up period after power-up before readings stabilize because their internal heater needs time to reach operating temperature. The datasheet will specify the recommended warm-up time — follow it to avoid false positives or drift. Another practical point is that MQ sensors often provide relative readings rather than calibrated parts-per-million values; many projects use them for threshold detection, like triggering an alarm when values exceed a baseline. A frequent misconception is assuming an immediate, absolute concentration reading: instead, treat MQ readings as comparative signals and allow for calibration and warm-up to determine a safe threshold for your application. Use MQ-2 for alarms or relative air-quality measurements, then choose thresholds based on observed baseline readings after warm-up.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Keep these three ideas front and center as you work with environmental sensors. First, know whether a sensor is analog or digital. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on the everyday sensors you’ll use to sense temperature, humidity, light, and common gases. You will learn what each sensor measures, how it represents that measurement as a voltage or a digital message, and why reading the right signal matters when you convert a number into degrees, percent, or a safety alert. We’ll use analog examples like the TMP36 and LM35 that give a voltage proportional to temperature, and digital examples like the DHT11 and DHT22 that send humidity and temperature as a timed data packet. You’ll also see how an LDR works inside a voltage divider to report light, and how an MQ-2 reports gas concentration on an analog output after a warm-up period. I’ll explain where a datasheet gives you the conversion formulas, and how a library safely hides timing details for digital sensors. By the end of this chapter you’ll be able to wire a sensor, choose analog versus digital reading, install a library, and convert raw readings into a human-friendly value. Think about a simple weather logger or a safety alarm — these are direct applications of what you’ll build here.

These four objectives give you practical, testable skills. First, you will interface with analog temperature sensors like the TMP36 and LM35 so you can convert a measured voltage into degrees Celsius. This matters because raw voltages are not intuitive until you apply the sensor's scale and offset from the datasheet. Second, you will use digital sensors such as the DHT11 and DHT22 to read temperature and humidity using a library. The library handles precise timing and produces reliable values; you will learn how to install and call the functions in your sketch. Third, you will read light levels using a light-dependent resistor inside a voltage divider. That teaches you how resistance maps to voltage and how simple calibration produces percentages or thresholds for real projects. Fourth, you will learn to use sensor datasheets and libraries: how to find conversion formulas, warm-up requirements, and wiring notes so your measurements are accurate and repeatable. Each objective includes a practical milestone so you can verify competency and build a simple monitoring circuit confidently.

You will apply the objectives by wiring sensors, installing libraries, and converting readings to human-friendly values. For analog temperature sensors you will show you can calculate Celsius from a voltage reading and explain the difference between sensors with an offset versus those without. For DHT sensors you will install the DHT library through the Arduino Library Manager and run an example that prints humidity and temperature to the Serial Monitor every two seconds. For light sensing, you will wire an LDR in a voltage divider and demonstrate a threshold that toggles a virtual or physical indicator for light versus dark. Finally, you will locate conversion details in a datasheet and explain why a gas sensor like the MQ-2 needs warm-up time before reliable readings. These milestones help you test hardware and software together, and they form the basis for the hands-on activity that follows in this chapter.

Sensors present the physical world as electrical values in two common forms: analog voltages or digital data. An analog sensor changes its output voltage continuously as the measured quantity changes. For example, the TMP36 outputs a voltage that rises linearly with temperature. The Arduino’s analog-to-digital converter samples that voltage and turns it into an integer between zero and 1023 on a five-volt board. Digital sensors, like the DHT11 and DHT22, transmit encoded data over a single wire in timed pulses rather than presenting a continuous voltage. The microcontroller needs to follow that protocol or use a library that does. The practical difference matters when you wire and read the part: analog sensors typically need a stable reference, and digital sensors need correct timing or a library. A common misconception is that all sensors can be read with analogRead; digital sensors require protocol handling. A quick example: the TMP36’s analog voltage can be converted directly into degrees using the datasheet formula, while a DHT11 requires a library call that returns humidity and temperature. Takeaway: choose the read method that matches the sensor’s signal type so your code and wiring produce meaningful numbers.

The TMP36 is an analog temperature sensor whose output is a voltage that changes linearly with temperature. The datasheet gives two important facts: at 25 degrees Celsius the output is 750 millivolts, and the sensor scales approximately 10 millivolts per degree. Practically, on a standard five-volt Arduino, you read an ADC value, convert it to a voltage by dividing by 1023 and multiplying by five, then apply the TMP36 formula. For example, subtract the 500 millivolt offset and multiply by 100 to get degrees Celsius. A common misunderstanding is to forget the offset; using the wrong formula will shift every reading by several degrees. The example code shown produces an integer reading, computes voltage, then temperature in Celsius. Try the short mental test: given 0.73 volts from a TMP36, the formula leads to 23 degrees C when you subtract 0.5 and multiply by 100. This screen shows the code and explains each step so you can confidently translate ADC numbers into human-friendly temperatures. In practical terms, convert adc reading to celsius with the tmp36 scale. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

TMP36 and LM35 are both analog temperature sensors commonly used with Arduino, and both scale at about 10 millivolts per degree Celsius. The crucial practical difference is the presence of an offset with the TMP36 and none with the LM35. The TMP36 specifies an offset so its output is roughly 0.5 volts at zero degrees, which simplifies single-supply designs but requires you to subtract that offset when converting voltage to temperature. The LM35, on the other hand, has no offset: its output is near 0 volts at zero degrees, so you multiply the measured voltage by the scale directly. When choosing between them, consult the datasheet for accuracy, operating voltage, and wiring notes — which tells you the correct formula to use. DHT11 and DHT22 are digital humidity and temperature sensors that communicate over a single data wire using timed pulses. They are not analog voltage outputs, so you cannot use analogRead. Instead, you either implement the precise timing protocol yourself or — more commonly — use a library that handles the timing and parsing for you. An LDR changes its resistance depending on the light level: more light usually reduces resistance, while darkness increases it.
